analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to take federal oil and gas royalties as physical oil and gas rather than cash.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee approved the bill by voice vote on June 18, 1998, but the full Natural Resources Committee never acted, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal government to take its share of oil and gas from federal and offshore leases as physical product ("in kind") instead of cash, then hire private marketing agents to sell it. It would relieve the companies leasing that land of most royalty reporting duties, reimburse them for transporting the government's share, keep their transportation charges confidential, and set aside 40% of government royalty oil for small refiners at a discount. Supporters said taking physical oil would end fights over whether companies were paying fair value; the bill's design also shifted real costs and information advantages to the companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies leasing federal and outer continental shelf lands gain the most: they would only have to make the oil and gas available at the lease, with no duty to market the government's share, no royalty-value reporting or recordkeeping under the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act, reimbursement from the Treasury for transporting the government's share, and confidentiality for their transportation charges and any arbitration over them. Small refiners (capacity under 100,000 barrels per day) gain a guaranteed 40% share of government royalty oil priced at the weighted average of the lowest successful offers, plus an advisory panel. Marketing and trading firms gain new government contracts to sell the oil, paid out of royalty proceeds without a separate appropriation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal oil and gas lessees and small refiners

how_it_helps.text: Lessee companies would be freed from any obligation to market, process, or bear downstream liability for the government's share of production once it is tendered at the delivery point.

Lessees would be exempt from the royalty reporting and recordkeeping requirements of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act for volumes taken in kind, and the Secretary's audit right would be limited to verifying volumes, not values.

The United States, not the lessee, would bear transportation costs for the royalty share, reimbursing companies at tariff rates or, for their own unregulated pipelines, cost-plus rates with a return pegged to BBB bond rates — with the charges kept confidential.

Eligible small refiners would be guaranteed 40% of government royalty oil, priced off the weighted average of the lowest 40% of successful offers, with creditworthiness terms capped at standard industry requirements and an advisory panel to shape the rules.
Taking royalties in kind could protect taxpayers from undervaluation disputes: the net proceeds of the government's own sales would be deemed to satisfy fair market value requirements by law.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury: the government would pay all transportation (including compression and dehydration), processing, and marketing-agent costs out of royalty proceeds, and would bear the discount built into the small-refiner set-aside. States receiving royalty shares would share those net receipts. Because lessee transportation charges and arbitration outcomes would be confidential and value reporting would be stripped away, the public would also lose visibility into how much its oil is worth.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury and state royalty recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill transfers gathering-and-transport economics to the public side: the United States must pay to move, process, and market the royalty share, and companies' own pipelines would be reimbursed at cost-plus rates — up to twice the BBB bond rate as a return — while the charges themselves stay confidential.

Value oversight is weakened: lessees are exempted from royalty-value reporting and FOGRMA recordkeeping, and the Secretary's audit authority is limited to volumes, so disputes over what the oil was worth would be replaced by a legal presumption that the government's own sale price is fair market value.
Disputes over pipeline charges would go to binding, confidential arbitration whose results no party may disclose, with production protected from delay while disputes run.

The small-refiner set-aside is priced off the lowest 40% of offers — a structural discount — and the bill repeals the existing royalty-in-kind authority rather than adding to it, so if mandatory in-kind proved costly there would be no fallback.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — government selling its own oil instead of litigating its value — had real merit in an era when royalty undervaluation was a live dispute, and taking royalties in kind could genuinely end those fights. But the bill is built with a heavy thumb on the industry's side of the scale: the treasury absorbs transport and processing costs at cost-plus rates, lessee charges and arbitrations stay secret, value reporting and value audits are stripped out, and a 40% slice of royalty oil is set aside at a structural discount. An honest supporter would concede the bill's costs and information losses could plausibly exceed its valuation gains; the design gives little confidence the net effect favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got hearings and a subcommittee voice vote, but the full House committee never took it up and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the Royalty Enhancement Act on March 4, 1998, with Reps. Cubin and Brady as original cosponsors; it was referred to the House Committee on Resources.
Three days later it went to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and Interior was asked for its comments.
The subcommittee held hearings on March 19 and May 21, 1998, then amended the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote on June 18, 1998.
No further action appears in the record: no full-committee markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal oil and gas lessees, who kept the existing cash-royalty system with none of the bill's new tendering obligations — while taxpayers also kept the existing royalty-in-value rules and audit authority rather than taking on the bill's transportation costs and confidentiality provisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal lessees, who avoided new tendering rules

for.name: Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 4, 1998 to convert federal oil and gas royalties to in-kind collection.

for.name: 10 House cosponsors (9 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Cubin and Brady.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
for.role: Subcommittee of the Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held two hearings (March 19 and May 21, 1998), amended the bill, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote on June 18, 1998.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Full committee of jurisdiction — never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the subcommittee forwarded the amended bill on June 18, 1998; the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist; sponsorship was nearly all Republican (9 of 10 cosponsors were Republicans, with 1 Democrat), and the only recorded approval was a subcommittee voice vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers leasing federal and offshore lands
industries.note: The bill would shed their duty to market the government's share, exempt them from royalty-value reporting and most FOGRMA recordkeeping, reimburse them for transporting the government's oil at tariff or cost-plus rates, and keep those charges and any arbitration confidential. Their gains come at public expense: treasury-borne transport costs and the loss of value oversight.

industries.industry: Small refiners (under 100,000 barrels per day capacity)
industries.note: A guaranteed 40% of government royalty oil would be offered to them at prices pegged to the lowest 40% of successful offers, with creditworthiness terms capped at standard industry practice and an advisory panel of their representatives shaping the rules. The discount is a carve-out paid out of royalty receipts that the public and states share.

industries.industry: Oil and gas marketing and trading firms
industries.note: They would win new government contracts to receive, transport, and sell the royalty share, paid from royalty proceeds without further appropriation, with one exclusive agent per lease for oil and one for gas. Affiliates of lessees could qualify if the Secretary found no conflict.

industries.industry: Large refiners (over 100,000 barrels per day capacity)
industries.note: They would be barred from the 40% small-refiner set-aside, though still free to bid on open sales; the effect on them is modest since most royalty oil would remain competitively offered.

industries.industry: Oil and gas pipelines and transporters
industries.note: The government would become a paying shipper of royalty volumes at tariff rates, and companies' own unregulated pipelines would be reimbursed at cost-plus rates with a guaranteed return — a new revenue stream paid from public royalty proceeds, with the charges kept confidential.
